Mire
mīre
n. (deep mud; the emblem of a place with no footing; rendering Hebrew tit, yaven)
From Old Norse myrr, a bog. Scripture's interest in mire is not that it is dirty but that it offers no standing — a man in it cannot get purchase.

Biblical Definition

Mire is deep mud, and its terror in Scripture is the absence of a floor. The psalmist's cry is exact: “I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing” (Psa 69:2), and the prayer follows, “Deliver me out of the mire, and let me not sink” (Psa 69:14) — a psalm the New Testament applies repeatedly to Christ. Jeremiah lives the figure literally: lowered by cords into a dungeon where “there was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire” (Jer 38:6) — the prophet of God at the bottom of a cistern for telling the truth. Job says God has cast him into it (Job 30:19). And Isaiah gives the diagnosis that turns the image inward: “the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt” (Isa 57:20) — the mire is not only what a man sinks into but what an unquiet heart throws up.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines mire as deep mud, earth so wet as to be soft and adhesive — and as a verb, to plunge or fix in mire, to set fast in mud.

expand to see more

MIRE, n. Deep mud; earth so wet and soft as to yield to the feet and to wheels.

MIRE, v.t. To plunge and fix in mire; to set or stall in mud.

2. To soil or daub with mud or foul matter.

MIRE, v.i. To sink in mud, or to sink so deep as to be unable to move forward.

Key Scripture

Psa 69:2 — "I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing: I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me."

Jer 38:6 — "Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech, that was in the court of the prison: and they let down Jeremiah with cords. And in the dungeon there was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire."

Isa 57:20 — "But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt."

Psa 69:14 — "Deliver me out of the mire, and let me not sink: let me be delivered from them that hate me, and out of the deep waters."

Modern Corruption

Restlessness sold as ambition and treated as a virtue, where Isaiah names it the mark of the wicked — a sea that cannot rest, casting up mire and dirt.

expand to see more

Isaiah 57:20 diagnoses a condition the age admires. The troubled sea cannot rest, and what it produces is mire and dirt — the churning itself is the problem, and the filth is a by-product of the restlessness. A culture that measures a life by its striving, and that cannot tolerate stillness for the length of a meal, has made a virtue of exactly what the prophet names as the estate of the wicked. And the verse ends with the sentence that explains it: there is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked.

The pastoral half is Psalm 69, and it is the psalm of the Man of Sorrows. I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing. Whatever a believer means by that sentence, Christ meant it first and more deeply, which is why the psalm can be prayed honestly by anyone in it. Jeremiah's cistern makes the same point historically: the man in the mire was not being punished for unfaithfulness but suffering for it, and the man who drew him out did it with old rags and cords, one act of ordinary kindness in a collapsing city.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tit (H2916), mud, clay, mire; yaven (H3121), deep mire, the sinking kind — used in Psa 69:2; bots (H1206), mire, marsh.

expand to see more

Hebrew tit (H2916) — mud, mire, clay; trodden like the mire of the streets (Isa 10:6) and cast up by the troubled sea (Isa 57:20).

Hebrew yaven (H3121) — deep, sinking mire; used only twice, both in the Psalms, both of a man with no footing (Psa 40:2; Psa 69:2).

Hebrew bor (H953) — a pit, cistern; Jeremiah's dungeon with no water but mire (Jer 38:6), and the pit from which Psa 40:2 lifts a man to a rock.

Usage

"“I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing” — the terror is the missing floor."

"“There was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire” — the prophet at the bottom."

"“The wicked are like the troubled sea… whose waters cast up mire and dirt”."
